title: Vectors (part 4)
textbookText: Now, think that while you're in that town, you're suddenly lost at some weird intersection. You know that there's a path from the place you came from, A and another path to a place, C and all you know is that these roads are at the right angle to B, your destination. Take a cross product and voila! You have the road that you need to take to get to B before the sun sets and the dinner gets cold.

As for why the dot product of two vectors is scalar, you just need to brush up on the definition of the dot product. It is only when you disregard the directions and consider the magnitude (length) of the vectors, multiply them with each other, and then with the cosine of angle between them, you get a dot product. There's no direction here. Now where would I need it in real life? How about if I want to find out how much water is rushing through that little hole in the faucet? I would take the flow of water in different outward directions from the hole as vectors and use the dot product to find how much of it I am losing. 2.6.1 Scalar Products: For any two vectors A⃗⃗ and⃗⃗B⃗⃗, the scalar product (Or the dot product), denoted by A⃗⃗⃗⃗. Here the product ⃗⃗A⃗⃗⃗. B⃗⃗ = AB cosθ always yields a scalar quantity and hence the name scalar product (or the dot product).
